title: Working with Data at Scale
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter answers a practical question: once a dataset, or a computation on it, no longer fits comfortably inside a single Python or R process on a laptop, what tools exist for computing in parallel, for storing and querying data too large for memory, and for getting data down from the web in the first place? It assumes familiarity with basic Unix tools (`grep`, `awk`, pipes), with `pandas`/`numpy`, and with the general idea of a data frame. The material is drawn from three different years of the same course unit slot, since what "Unit 7" covered changed from year to year: in 2021 it was the concepts of parallel computing; in 2024-2025 it was MapReduce-style tools for big data — Dask, Hadoop, Spark, and databases; in 2026 it was acquiring and encoding data from the web (material that in earlier years lived in a different unit). They are presented here as one connected arc — get the data, compute on it at scale, store and query it — rather than as unrelated lectures. ## Before reaching for exotic tools "Big data" was a genuine buzzword for a while, and some of the hype around giant datasets is justified and some of it is not. Large datasets let you address questions smaller datasets can't, and they let you consider more sophisticated (e.g., nonlinear) relationships. But size alone does not solve two much older problems. First, correlation is still not causation: having medical records on every American doesn't tell you whether higher salt intake causes hypertension, and a huge log of website clicks doesn't tell you whether a feature *caused* more sales — that still needs a designed experiment, or careful causal reasoning about observational data. Second, an ad hoc "sample" is not a statistical sample, and a big pile of unrepresentative data does not let you infer properties of a population — this is exactly why answering questions about Covid was so hard despite enormous amounts of data: the data were incomplete and non-representative. A well-chosen *smaller* dataset can be far more informative than a much larger, ad hoc one. What a big dataset can buy you is the ability to select a genuinely representative sub-sample, or to get closer to a causal effect — but that takes deliberate design, not just volume. Big datasets also invite a large number of statistical tests, so multiple testing becomes a serious issue: with enough analyses, something will look interesting purely by chance. (For two documented examples of this kind of bias in analyses of electronic health records, see [Foraita et al.](https://doi.org/10.1093/jrsssa/qnae039) and [a second study](https://doi.org/10.1093/jrsssa/qnae005).) People also define "big" differently — sometimes by literal size (and speed of collection), sometimes by how pervasive data-backed analysis has become in a domain, regardless of the size of any one dataset. The tools below target the first sense, and specifically datasets that are large by the standards of ordinary statistical work — gigabytes to tens of gigabytes — but nowhere near what Google or a national security agency would call large. ### Why memory is the bottleneck Python and R keep objects in memory, so a session cannot directly work with a dataset much bigger than about 1-20 GB, depending on the machine. The tools in this chapter (short of a full database or cluster) target that gigabytes-to-tens-of-gigabytes range; they can scale further given enough memory, disk, and patience. Past hundreds of gigabytes or into terabytes/petabytes, a properly administered database, a cloud platform (AWS, GCP), or Spark are the realistic options. A general rule when handling big files: keep the data on local disk on the machine doing the computing, since moving it over the network is slow. ### What plain tools already buy you Before reaching for a distributed system, it's worth remembering what's already fast. Unix commands and pipes are quick, and `grep`, `head`, `tail`, and `awk` let you filter rows or extract columns without loading anything into Python or R. [GNU parallel](https://docs-research-it.berkeley.edu/services/high-performance-computing/user-guide/running-your-jobs/gnu-parallel/) parallelizes shell commands and is a common way to use a cluster's cores from the command line. Simple discipline helps too: if a 10 GB file has 30 columns and you need 5, drop the rest before doing anything else; a random sample of a huge dataset may answer your question as well as the full thing. Storing data in a binary format instead of flat text (CSV) also shrinks it considerably. For many applications, simply putting the data in a standard database (below) is enough. ## Concepts for parallel computation Some recurring situations in applied statistics motivate parallel computing directly: fitting several models to the same data, running the same model on each of several cross-validation folds, running stratified analyses across many subgroups, or running a simulation study with many replicates. What makes these amenable to parallel processing is that the individual pieces of work don't need to talk to each other while running — the iterations can be farmed out, run on their own, and their results collected at the end. This is called an **embarrassingly parallel (EP)** problem: simulations with independent replicates, bootstrapping, stratified analysis, random forests, and cross-validation are all standard statistical examples. Given $p$ CPUs, an EP problem can, apart from some overhead, run in roughly $1/p$ the time of the serial version — a *linear speedup*, so called because the speedup is (approximately) proportional to $p$. Some vocabulary that recurs throughout this material: - **core**: a processing unit on a single machine or node. - **node**: one computer (with its own memory) in a cluster or supercomputer. - **process**: a running instance of a program; a program may launch several. - **worker**: a process actually doing part of a parallelized computation. - **task**: an individual unit of work assigned to a process. - **thread**: a path of execution inside a single process; the OS sees one process, but a threaded computation can use more than 100% of a CPU by running on several cores at once. - **forking**: spawning a child process that starts as a copy of the parent (same memory, until something changes) — cheap, because unmodified objects need not be copied. - **scheduler**: the software that allocates jobs to nodes on a shared cluster. - **load-balanced**: every core assigned to a computation stays busy for its whole duration. ### Shared vs. distributed memory There are two basic architectures. In **shared memory**, several cores on one machine or node all see the same memory, so there's no need to explicitly send data between them — though unless you use threads (or forked processes that haven't modified their inherited objects), a new process still gets its own copy of the data. In **distributed memory**, each node has its own separate memory, and nodes are connected by a network; moving data from one node's memory to another's requires explicitly passing messages (the standard protocol is MPI). The practical consequence is that communication between a core and its own memory is much faster than communication between cores on different nodes, so the cost of a parallel scheme depends heavily on how much data has to cross that boundary. A large supercomputer like NERSC's Cori has thousands of nodes (12,076, with 735,200 cores total), each with its own 96-128 GB of memory (1.3 PB combined) — communication *within* one node is cheap, but shuffling data across all those nodes is not. Two other approaches are worth naming, though the course only touched on them briefly. **GPUs** hold a very large number of simple processing units for massively parallel calculation, and most people use them indirectly, through machine-learning software (TensorFlow, PyTorch, Caffe) that has already been written to exploit one when available. **Cloud computing** (AWS EC2, Google Compute Engine, Azure) rents access to virtual machines with a chosen number of cores, configured and used like an ordinary machine, and which can be assembled into your own virtual cluster — including one running Spark. Hadoop and Spark themselves (next section) are the MapReduce-based way of using a distributed-memory cluster. ## MapReduce, Hadoop, and Spark For roughly the last twenty years, the alternative to classic message-passing HPC (MPI-style) has been technologies that spread a dataset across many machines but let you manipulate it as if it were one. The general recipe for this is the **MapReduce** paradigm: 1. Read individual records (e.g., lines of a CSV, or whole files). 2. **Map**: turn each input record into a key-value pair (more formally, map takes a key-value pair and returns a new one) — records are treated completely independently here. 3. **Reduce**: for each key, combine all its associated values into one result — keys are treated completely independently here too. 4. Write out each {key, result} pair. Because the map step only ever looks at one record and the reduce step only ever looks at one key's worth of values, every step can run in parallel across many machines. Within that constraint you can still do sophisticated things: a map function can drop values, transform them, or emit several records from one input; a reduce function can carry out fairly involved computation on the values that land on it. (`pandas` and `dplyr`'s [split-apply-combine strategy](http://www.jstatsoft.org/v40/i01/paper) is the same idea under a different name.) The one operation to watch for is anything that needs to move a lot of data between workers to compute — a **shuffle**. Computing a *median* within groups whose members are scattered across workers requires gathering all of a group's values together, which can be slow; computing a *mean* or *sum*, by contrast, only requires each worker to send back a small partial sum, which is cheap. **Hadoop** is an infrastructure that runs MapReduce over a network of machines, hiding the work of distributing computation and collecting results. It bundles a distributed file system, HDFS, which stores each piece of data redundantly across several machines; computation is done where the data already lives, which limits network traffic, and if a node fails, Hadoop reruns its tasks elsewhere. It's written in Java, and setting up a cluster is enough work that, realistically, you'd expect to be handed a running one rather than building it yourself. **Spark** can be thought of as *in-memory Hadoop*: it treats the combined memory of multiple nodes as one large pool, so it's faster than Hadoop whenever the data fits in that collective memory, and falls back to reading from HDFS (which is usually where it starts from anyway) when it doesn't. It's more user-friendly than Hadoop but still non-trivial: cluster setup takes work, performance tuning is fiddly, and Spark jobs have a habit of failing — often on memory — in ways that are hard to debug. Spark is included here for reference; the course's hands-on tool for this material is Dask. ## Dask for big-data processing Dask parallelizes computation across chunks (also called *partitions* or *shards*) of a dataset, using multiple cores on one machine or across several. Like Spark, it reads files in parallel and processes them a chunk at a time, which buys two things: the reading and computing themselves run in parallel, and — because each worker only ever needs one chunk in memory — a dataset that doesn't fit in memory on one machine can still be processed, especially once spread across several machines' memory. (Reading many chunks off one physical disk at once runs into the disk's own bandwidth limits; real parallel file systems, or Hadoop/Spark's practice of spreading data over one disk per node, avoid this.) Because heavy numeric work happens in compiled code (`numpy` underneath), it's usually best to use Dask's `threads` scheduler on a single node, so data doesn't have to be copied between workers. Dask offers three structures built on this idea: - **Dask dataframes** are Pandas-like, split into row-groups that are each an ordinary Pandas dataframe; by default they use the `threads` scheduler. Reading an 11 GB flight-delay dataset from a folder of compressed CSVs looks like ordinary Pandas, but nothing is actually read until a result is requested: ```python import dask.dataframe as ddf air = ddf.read_csv(path + '*.csv.bz2', compression='bz2', encoding='latin1', dtype={'Distance': 'float64', 'DepDelay': 'float64'}) air.DepDelay.mean().compute() # triggers the actual read and computation sub = air[(air.UniqueCarrier == 'UA') & (air.Origin == 'SFO')] sub.groupby('Dest').DepDelay.mean().compute() # a split-apply-combine, i.e. MapReduce, query ``` Because of the *lazy evaluation* used here, reading and every later operation (`max`, `groupby`, `mean`) only happen once `.compute()` is called — and calling `.compute()` a second time re-reads the data from scratch, so it's worth building up the whole chain of operations before calling it once. Dask also refuses to compute a `median` in this setting, for the same shuffle reason MapReduce does. And whatever `.compute()` returns comes back as an ordinary, fully in-memory Python object on one process — easy to accidentally ask for something enormous. - **Dask bags** behave like unordered lists (there is no "i'th element") and are handled by the `processes` scheduler by default; they are the parallel-map analogue for data that isn't yet structured, such as raw lines of a Wikipedia log file: ```python wiki = db.read_text(path + 'part-0*gz') wiki.filter(find).count().compute() # find() is an ordinary Python predicate df = wiki.filter(find).map(make_tuple).to_dataframe(dtypes) # then structure it ``` As with dataframes, chaining `filter`, `map`, and other steps before a single `compute()` avoids redundant reads. - **Dask arrays** are numpy-like, split into blocks along both axes, and handled by `threads` by default. A telling demonstration: computing row means of an 80 GB random array never uses more than a few GB of memory, because Dask generates and discards chunks on the fly rather than materializing the whole array; and, somewhat counterintuitively, chunking by full rows versus by square blocks made no real difference to the time taken for a row-mean calculation, since only a small summary (the partial mean) needs to move between workers either way. ## Databases and SQL A relational database is a set of rectangular tables (*relations*), each with typed columns (*fields*/*attributes*) and rows (*records*), much like a data frame — except several tables typically share fields, so information gets **joined** (merged) across them, and the database is built to make that querying and joining fast. Formally, a database lives on disk rather than in memory, which sounds like it should be slow — but operating-system disk caching and well-implemented database algorithms often make it fast in practice. You interact with a database (a *DBMS*, or database management system — SQLite, DuckDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, ...) using SQL, a special-purpose language for querying and managing relational data; the syntax varies a little between systems, but the core is shared. Many DBMS use a client-server model: clients authenticate to a server and send it queries. **SQLite** and **DuckDB** are simpler — self-contained, no server, just one file on disk that you connect to from a shell, R, or Python — though they lack some features of the full client-server systems (e.g., SQLite can't `ALTER TABLE` to change or drop a column). **DuckDB** additionally stores data *column-wise*, which speeds up queries that scan large parts of a table (so-called OLAP-style analytics), and can operate on on-disk data without pulling it all into memory. ### Designing a schema: normalization Getting real value from a database means **normalizing** the data — spreading it across several tables so that no piece of information is repeated unnecessarily. The database's *schema* is just the metadata describing which tables exist and which typed fields each one has. Take a school database with many teachers, many classes, and many students. Put everything in one table, one row per student, and you'd need repeated groups of fields for however many classes a student could take — class 1, grade in class 1, teacher 1 ID, teacher 1 name, teacher 1 department, teacher 1 age, class 2, grade in class 2, ... — with the whole block copied per class slot. Putting one row per student per class instead removes the repeated groups but keeps a different flaw. Either way, a teacher's age or department gets repeated once for every student in every one of their classes, and it would only get worse if a teacher could belong to several departments at once (a so-called *multivalued dependency*), since then every student-class-teacher combination would be crossed with every one of that teacher's departments. The fix is to give each kind of entity its own table: - **Student**: ID, name, grade_level - **Teacher**: ID, name, department, age - **Class**: ID, topic, class_size, teacher_ID - **Enrollment**: student_ID, class_ID, grade `Enrollment` has one row per student-class pair, which is exactly how you handle "ragged" data (a variable number of classes per student) — the same pattern behind "tidy", long-format data. A **key** is a field, or set of fields, that's unique per row; each table's **primary key** is its main identifier (`Student.ID`, `Teacher.ID`, `Class.ID`, and, for `Enrollment`, the pair `{student_ID, class_ID}`), and a **foreign key** is a column in one table holding another table's primary key value — `Enrollment.student_ID` referencing `Student.ID`, `Class.teacher_ID` referencing `Teacher.ID`, and so on. Joining tables means matching a foreign key in one to the primary key in another, e.g. to get the grades of every 9th-grader: ```sql SELECT Student.ID, grade FROM Student, Enrollment WHERE Student.ID = Enrollment.student_ID AND Student.grade_level = 9; ``` (If a normalized schema always ends up being recombined the same way for every query, a single, deliberately denormalized table — or a *view*, a saved query usable as if it were a table — may be the more practical choice. It is possible to be too pure about normalization.) ### A worked example: Stack Overflow The course used a real, normalized database of Stack Overflow question/answer metadata for 2021, with tables `questions` (questionid, creationdate, score, viewcount, answercount, commentcount, favoritecount, title, ownerid), `answers` (answerid, questionid, creationdate, score, ownerid), `users` (userid, creationdate, lastaccessdate, location, reputation, displayname, upvotes, downvotes, age, accountid), and `questions_tags` (questionid, tag). From Python you connect and query it directly with SQL: ```python import sqlite3 as sq con = sq.connect('stackoverflow-2021.db') db = con.cursor() db.execute("select title, viewcount from questions order by viewcount desc limit 10").fetchall() ``` or return a Pandas dataframe directly with `pandas.read_sql("select ...", con)`. SQL is *declarative* — you say what result you want and let the DBMS figure out how — unlike the *imperative* style of most of the languages used elsewhere in this course. The core query shape is ```sql SELECT FROM WHERE ORDER BY ``` with `WHERE` supporting `LIKE`, `IN`, `=`, `<`, `>`, etc.; other important keywords include `DISTINCT`, `JOIN`/`ON`, `GROUP BY`, `AS`, `USING`, `UNION`, `INTERSECT`. **Grouping.** `GROUP BY` splits a table into mutually exclusive, exhaustive subsets and applies an aggregate (`COUNT`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `AVG`, `SUM`) to each — one output row per group: ```sql SELECT tag, COUNT(*) AS n FROM questions_tags GROUP BY tag ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT 25; ``` (Filtering *after* a `GROUP BY` needs `HAVING`, not `WHERE`.) `DISTINCT` removes duplicate rows or values, e.g. `SELECT DISTINCT tag FROM questions_tags`. **Joins.** The general shape is `SELECT ... FROM t1 JOIN t2 ON WHERE ... ORDER BY ...`, and it can be written several equivalent ways: ```sql select * from table1 join table2 on table1.id = table2.id; -- explicit inner join select * from table1, table2 where table1.id = table2.id; -- same thing, no JOIN keyword select * from table1 cross join table2 where table1.id = table2.id; -- cross join, then filter select * from table1 join table2 using(id); -- explicit, shorthand key name ``` Three-way joins work the same way, chaining `ON`/`WHERE` conditions across all three tables. There are three flavors, distinguished by how they handle rows on one side with no match on the other: an **inner join** keeps only matched rows (e.g., only questions that have at least one answer); a **left (or right, or full) outer join** additionally keeps unmatched rows from the left (right, both) table, filling the missing side with `NULL` — so a left outer join of questions with answers would include questions with zero answers; and a **cross join** returns the full Cartesian product of both tables (every row of one paired with every row of the other), which for two big tables can be very large. An inner join can itself be seen as a cross join followed by a filter down to the matching rows. **Indexes.** An index orders a table's rows by one or more fields so the DBMS can look values up without scanning every row. Without an index, a lookup is $O(n)$ in the number of rows $n$; a tree-based index gives $O(\log n)$ lookup, and a hash-based index can give $O(1)$ — but only for exact matches, since a hash index is built by hashing the indexed value(s), so a *range* query (e.g. `viewcount > 10000`) needs a tree-based index instead. Building an index itself costs time, so it's only worth it if you'll run enough queries against that column to recoup the cost. **Set operations and subqueries.** `UNION`, `INTERSECT`, and `EXCEPT` apply set operations to tables (or single columns) with matching schemas — e.g. intersecting "users who asked a question" with "users who answered a question" finds people who did both, more directly than the equivalent join. A **subquery** is a full query nested inside another — in the `FROM` clause, to build a temporary table to join against, or in the `WHERE` clause, to test membership in a set the subquery defines (with `IN` or `NOT IN`). For a complex query it's often easier to first write and check the subquery as a standalone view, then fold it back in — for a large database you generally want the final version to run as one query rather than two, so the SQL optimizer can plan across the whole thing. Finally, a table can be created directly from a dataframe: `student_data.to_sql('student', con, if_exists='replace', index=False)`. ## Recent tools and storage formats Outside formal databases, large datasets are increasingly kept as collections of files — often Parquet or CSV — an arrangement referred to as a *data lake* when it lives in the cloud. **Apache Arrow** (`PyArrow` in Python) is a columnar in-memory format: values within a column sit contiguously, so a specific value can be fetched in $O(1)$ time without touching the rest of the column. Arrow reads from Parquet, its own native format, and plain text, and — like Dask — only pulls in the data it actually needs from disk, keeping memory and I/O down (the native Arrow format is best on this count). **Polars** is a fast Pandas alternative built on the Arrow columnar format, with a lazy execution model similar to Dask's or Spark's that lets it optimize a whole chain of operations before running any of it. Many statistical methods produce or rely on **sparse matrices** — most entries zero, so there's no need to store or compute with them. Examples include the neighborhood (conditional-dependence) structure of a graphical model, the neighborhood structure behind spatial or temporal autoregressive models, and the *lasso*, which is used specifically to produce sparse parameter or covariance estimates in high-dimensional problems. Python, R, and MATLAB all have dedicated sparse-matrix support (the technique is put to memorable use in [analyses of the Netflix Prize dataset](http://blog.revolutionanalytics.com/2011/05/the-neflix-prize-big-data-svd-and-r.html)). ## Getting data from the web Before any of the above tools matter, you often need to get the data in the first place. The `requests` package is the workhorse for this in Python (much of what follows can also be done from the shell with `curl` or `wget`). ### HTTP and REST APIs **HTTP** is the client-server protocol underlying the web: a client (e.g. your browser, or your script) sends a request and a server sends back a response, which carries a status code and content (HTML, XML, JSON, or raw bytes). Any URL with parameters after a `?` (`site.com?p1=a1&p2=a2`) is an API call. **REST** is the most common style of web API: you hit a URL (an *endpoint*) with a query string of `Parameter=Argument` pairs joined by `&` (spaces become `+`), generally via an HTTP GET request, and get back data in a documented format: ```python url = "https://api.worldbank.org/V2/country?incomeLevel=MIC&format=json" data = json.loads(requests.get(url).content) ``` — or built up programmatically from a dictionary of arguments, which scales better and is worth preferring once the query gets complicated. Watch for pagination (results silently truncated past some size, e.g. `per_page=1000`) and for authentication (an access token, or a browser-based login flow, e.g. for the Google Drive API); some services also support POST/PUT/DELETE for actions beyond reading, e.g. filing a GitHub issue via a POST request carrying a JSON body and a bearer token, or via a wrapper package (`PyGithub`) that hides the raw HTTP entirely. GET requests are capped in length (around 2048 characters by many servers); once a query gets too long to fit in a URL, a POST request is the way around it. Sometimes an API isn't documented at all. The recipe is then to reproduce, rather than read about, what your browser does: open the browser's network inspector (Firefox: Web Developer -> Network; Chrome: Developer tools -> Network), trigger the download by hand, find the actual GET request the browser sent, and reconstruct that URL programmatically. Downloading UN crop-production data this way returns a zip file (raw bytes), which then needs unzipping in memory before `pandas` can read the CSV inside it: ```python response = requests.get(url) # url reconstructed from the browser's network tab with io.BytesIO(response.content) as stream: with zipfile.ZipFile(stream) as archive: with archive.open(archive.filelist[0].filename) as file: dat = pd.read_csv(file) ``` This buys reproducibility (the whole thing can be handed to someone else, or rerun later) and lets you automate downloading many such files — at the cost that a small change to the website can silently break the query. **Webscraping ethics.** If a site offers a documented API or a plain downloadable file, use that in preference to scraping. If you must scrape, check what's actually permitted first: a site's Terms of Service, and its `robots.txt` (which states what an automated crawler may do, and often a required delay between requests — e.g. [Wikipedia's](https://wikitech.wikimedia.org/wiki/Robot_policy) or [Google Scholar's](https://scholar.google.com/robots.txt)); for heavy use, contact the site owner. Practically: cache the result of a request the first time and iterate on the processing code against the cached copy rather than re-requesting; add a delay between automated requests; and check the API's documentation for any published rate limit. ### Reading HTML, XML, JSON, and YAML **HTML**, viewed in a browser, is a rendering of an underlying text file; the same file can instead be parsed by code. `BeautifulSoup4` builds a tree of the document's elements (tags, nested and with attributes) that you can then search: ```python soup = bs(requests.get(url, headers=headers).content, 'html.parser') tables = [pd.read_html(io.StringIO(str(t)))[0] for t in soup.find_all('table')] links = [a.get('href') for a in soup.find_all('a', href=True)] ``` `soup.select(...)` supports [CSS selectors](https://www.w3schools.com/cssref/css_selectors.asp) (e.g. `"th > a"` for an `a` element whose parent is a `th`), and `lxml`'s XPath support (`doc.xpath('//a[@href]')`) gives a second, more powerful way to pick out elements — useful for HTML and for XML alike, since both have a tree structure of nested, tagged elements. **XML** is a self-describing, hierarchical markup format (used, e.g., as the underlying format for Office documents and for Google Earth's KML), where an element can carry attributes as well as nested child elements: ```xml Gambardella, Matthew XML Developer's Guide ``` `xmltodict` turns an XML document into nested Python dicts/lists directly; `lxml.etree` plus XPath (`doc.xpath("//loan")`, then `.xpath("location/country/text()")` on each match) is the more targeted route into a specific piece of a large document. **JSON** stores the same kind of hierarchical, key-value data more compactly than XML (no closing tags), with arrays in `[...]` and objects in `{...}`, and native `null`/boolean/number types — its one real gap being no standard way to represent something like infinity or a genuinely missing value. Python's `json.loads` turns it directly into nested dicts and lists. **YAML** is the lightweight format typically used for configuration (e.g. a GitHub Actions workflow), using indentation rather than brackets for nesting and no quoting for plain strings — readable, but correspondingly fragile, since indentation errors are easy to make and some values can be type-coerced in surprising ways (`on:` in a workflow file is parsed as the boolean `True` by PyYAML, a known quirk). `yaml.safe_load` reads a YAML file without executing any embedded code. ### Dynamic pages Some pages only produce their real content in reaction to Javascript or user interaction, and no amount of parsing the initial HTML will see it. For those you need something that drives an actual browser: `selenium`, or `scrapy` together with `splash`. ## File and string encodings Plain ASCII covers only $2^{7}=128$ characters and control codes — essentially a US keyboard — one byte (8 bits) each. The letter "M", for instance, is `01001101` in binary, or `4d` in hexadecimal (two nibbles, `0100` = `4` and `1101` = `d`); you can build an ASCII file directly from such hex bytes: ```python with open('tmp.txt', 'wb') as f: f.write(b'\x4d\x6f\x6d\x0a') # "Mom\n" ``` Once a file has characters outside that 128-character set — accents, non-Latin scripts — you need an **encoding**: a mapping from characters to numeric codes and then to bytes. The near-universal choice today is **Unicode** (over 110,000 characters, across around 100 scripts) as the numbering, encoded to bytes as **UTF-8**. A Unicode character's numeric ID is its *code point*, given in Python by `ord`. UTF-8's encoding is deliberately clever: ASCII characters still take one byte, most others take two, and some take four, and it's constructed so that the bit pattern of a one-byte character never appears inside the encoding of a longer one — the leading bits of a byte alone tell you how many bytes the character occupies. `ñ`, for example, has code point `\u00f1` (hex `f1`) but encodes to *two* UTF-8 bytes (`\xc3\xb1`). An older, narrower alternative is **Latin-1** (ISO 8859-1), which covers only 191 characters — ASCII plus the accented letters common in European languages — using exactly one byte each; the same `ñ` that needs two bytes in UTF-8 needs only one in Latin-1. This is precisely the kind of mismatch that produces decoding errors in practice: a file actually written in Latin-1, opened in Python (whose default encoding is UTF-8) without specifying `encoding='latin1'`, will fail or garble on its first non-ASCII byte. Python strings can be converted explicitly between encodings with `.encode(...)` (`text.encode('utf-8')`, `text.encode('latin1')`, and `text.encode('ascii')`, which raises on any character outside the 128-character range); the shell utility `iconv` and the Python `encode` function both handle conversions, and `file` on the command line will often report what encoding it guessed a given file is in. ## Exercises The Stack Overflow database used throughout has tables `questions` (questionid, creationdate, score, viewcount, answercount, commentcount, favoritecount, title, ownerid), `answers` (answerid, questionid, creationdate, score, ownerid), `users` (userid, creationdate, lastaccessdate, location, reputation, displayname, upvotes, downvotes, age, accountid), and `questions_tags` (questionid, tag). 1. Consider a school database recorded as a single table, one row per student, with repeated groups of fields — `class 1, grade in class 1, teacher ID 1, teacher name 1, teacher department 1, teacher age 1, class 2, grade in class 2, ...` — up to however many classes a student takes. What goes wrong with this design, and does putting one row per student-class pair instead (with the same fields, unrepeated) fix all of it? 2. Stack Overflow's question/answer/tag data could be put in one table with one row per question (with repeated tag and answer fields per question) or one row per question-answer pair (with repeated tag fields). Neither is a good schema. Design a normalized set of tables for this data. 3. Give a couple of ways to find the oldest users in the `users` table. How does the cost of each scale with the number of rows in the table? 4. Write a query that counts the number of answers for each question and returns the most-answered questions first. Why can this be done using only the `answers` table? 5. Write a query returning all the answers to questions tagged `'python'`. 6. Write a query returning the display names of the users who have answered a question tagged `'python'`. 7. Write a query (using `INTERSECT` or otherwise) to find the users who have neither asked nor answered a question. 8. Create a view with one row for every question-tag pair, including questions that have no tags at all. 9. Write a query returning the display names of all users who have never posted a question. (`NULL` plays the role of R's `NA`; think about which kind of join would produce it here.) 10. What does the following query compute? ```sql select * from questions join answers A on questions.questionid = A.questionid join (select ownerid, count(*) as n_answered from answers group by ownerid order by n_answered desc limit 1000) most_responsive on A.ownerid = most_responsive.ownerid ``` ## Sources - Berkeley STAT 243, fall-2025, Unit 7 "Big Data" (CC BY 4.0) — used as the primary text for this chapter's big-data material: preparatory notes and the editorial on big data (`01-1-a-few-preparatory-notes.md`); MapReduce, Hadoop, Spark, and Dask (`02-2-mapreduce-and-dask.md`); databases, schema design, and SQL (`03-3-databases.md`); recent tools, storage formats, and sparsity (`04-4-recent-tools-and-data-storage-formats.md`). - Berkeley STAT 243, fall-2024, the same unit a year earlier (CC BY 4.0) — `01-1-a-few-preparatory-notes.md`, `02-2-mapreduce-dask-hadoop-and-spark.md`, and `04-4-recent-tools-and-data-storage-formats.md`, consulted as a near-duplicate of the fall-2025 material; fall-2025's wording is used throughout as the clearer/updated version, per the once-only rule for material taught in more than one year (the two documented-bias citations in the editorial on big data appear only in fall-2025). - Berkeley STAT 243, fall-2026, Unit 7 "Data Tech" (CC BY 4.0) — this material occupied a different unit slot ("Unit 2") in the 2024/2025 offerings referenced above: overview (`01-overview.md`); working with information on the web — HTML, XML, JSON, YAML, HTTP, REST APIs, webscraping (`02-1-working-with-information-on-the-web.md`); file and string encodings (`03-2-file-and-string-encodings.md`). - Berkeley stat243-fall-2021, Unit 7 "Parallel" (CC0-1.0) — scenarios for parallelization and embarrassingly parallel problems (`01-1-some-scenarios-for-parallelization.md`); computer architecture, terminology, shared vs. distributed memory, GPUs, and cloud computing (`02-2-overview-of-parallel-processing.md`).
